blocks.prompt: The Robot That Never Gets Tired
blocks.text: A robot is a machine that can sense, think, and move. First it senses. A camera or a touch pad tells the robot what is around it. Then it thinks. A small computer inside works out what to do next. Then it moves. Motors turn the wheels or bend the arms. Sense, think, move. A robot does that loop over and over, very fast. People build robots to do jobs that are dull or dirty or dangerous. A robot arm can weld the same spot on a car ten thousand times. It never gets bored. It never needs a nap.

blocks.prompt: Where the Word Robot Came From
blocks.text: In 1920, a writer in Czechoslovakia named Karel Capek wrote a play about machines built to do all the hard work. He needed a name for them. His brother Josef suggested robota, an old Czech word for heavy, forced labor. Capek shortened it to robot. The word was born in a play, before any real robot existed. Forty one years later, the first one went to work. It was called Unimate. It was a heavy arm bolted to the floor of a car factory in New Jersey. Its job was to pick up hot pieces of metal and stack them. The metal was hot enough to burn a person. The arm did not care. It lifted the same piece the same way, all day and all night. That is what robots are for. People hand them the jobs that are dull, dirty, or dangerous. A robot will never get bored of a job. It will never look away at the wrong moment. But a robot is not just any arm. To count as a robot, a machine has to do three things: sense the world, decide what to do, and then move. Your toaster cannot do that. Unimate could, in a simple way. It knew where its own arm was, and it corrected itself when it drifted off target.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Three parts: sensors, controller, actuators
An encoder reports a joint's exact angle
Actuators are the muscles
The parts are wired in a circle, not a line
That circle is called a feedback loop
Some arms run the loop 1000 times a second

blocks.prompt: Sense, Think, Move
blocks.text: Open up a robot and you will find the same three parts every time, no matter what the robot is built for. The first part is sensors. A sensor is anything that turns the outside world into a number. A camera turns light into numbers. A microphone turns sound into numbers. A robot arm carries a sensor called an encoder on every joint, and the encoder reports the exact angle that joint is sitting at right now. The second part is the controller. This is the computer. It takes the numbers arriving from the sensors, compares them to the numbers it wants, and works out the difference. The third part is actuators. Actuators are the muscles: motors, pumps, anything that pushes. The controller sends power to the actuators, and the robot moves. Here is the important bit. Those three parts are wired in a circle, not a line. The robot moves, the sensors report what actually happened, and the controller adjusts. Then it does the whole thing again. A robot arm might run that circle a thousand times every second. The circle is called a feedback loop, and it is the whole secret. A machine without a feedback loop is just following orders and hoping. A machine with one can notice that it is wrong and fix itself while it works. That is the difference between a wind up toy and a robot. It is also why robots are patient in a way people are not. The loop does not get tired and it does not stop checking. A welding arm will place the same weld, to the same fraction of a millimeter, for eight hours, and the ten thousandth weld is as good as the first.

notes: Perseverance landed in Jezero Crater, 2021
A radio signal takes about 5 to 20 minutes each way
No live steering is possible
The rover maps the ground and picks its own route
Acting without being told is called autonomy
Spirit sank into soft soil in 2009

blocks.prompt: A Robot Alone on Mars
blocks.text: Right now there is a robot the size of a small car driving around on Mars. Its name is Perseverance. It landed in a crater called Jezero in February 2021, and no human being has touched it since. That last part is the problem. Mars is a long way off, and radio waves, fast as they are, still take time to cross the gap. Depending on where the two planets sit in their orbits, a signal from Earth needs somewhere between about five and twenty minutes to reach Mars. The reply takes just as long. So if the rover is rolling toward a hole, and a person on Earth sees it and shouts stop, the message arrives roughly ten minutes after the rover has already fallen in. You cannot drive a Mars rover the way you drive a remote control car. There is no live steering. Instead, the team on Earth sends the rover a plan for the day: head roughly that way, look at that rock. Then they go home. The rover fills in everything else by itself. So it does. Perseverance photographs the ground ahead, builds a rough map of what is safe and what is not, chooses a route through, drives a short distance, then stops and looks again. It repeats that all day. Nobody is watching. Nobody can help. That ability to act on a goal without being told each step is called autonomy, and on Mars it is not a luxury. It is the only thing that works. This is why space is such a demanding place to build robots for. On Earth, when a robot gets stuck, a person walks over and unsticks it. On Mars there is nobody to walk over. A rover that gets a wheel wedged in soft sand is finished, and that has happened. The rover Spirit sank into a patch of loose soil in 2009 and never drove again. A robot on Mars is not a tool that somebody is using. It is a machine that has been handed a task and left alone with it, further from help than anything people have ever built.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Deep Blue beat Garry Kasparov in 1997
Hans Moravec described the paradox in the 1980s
Hard for us is easy for machines, and the reverse
Modern chess is only about 500 years old
Grasping is hundreds of millions of years old
Nobody can write the rules for a sock

blocks.prompt: The Hardest Thing a Robot Can Do Is Pick Up a Sock
blocks.text: In 1997 a computer beat the best chess player alive. Garry Kasparov was the world champion, arguably the strongest the game had ever produced, and a machine called Deep Blue took a match off him. People treated it as a landmark, and it was. Chess is difficult. Chess is what clever looks like. Meanwhile, in a laboratory somewhere, a robot was struggling to pick a sock up off the floor. That gap has a name. The roboticist Hans Moravec described it in the 1980s, and it is now called Moravec's paradox: the things people find hard, machines find easy, and the things people find so easy that they do not count them as thinking at all, machines find nearly impossible. A computer can hold a chess position, a tax code, or the entire timetable of an airline in its head without effort. It cannot reliably pick up a sock. The reason is history. Modern chess is roughly five hundred years old. Human beings have been playing it, badly, for a few dozen generations, and we are not naturally built for it. When you play chess you are running a slow, conscious, effortful search. It feels like work because it is work, and your brain has no dedicated equipment for the task. Now think about what actually happens when you pick up a sock. Your eyes separate the sock from the carpet, a problem in shading and texture with no clean answer. You judge the distance. You choose, without noticing that you are choosing, where on the sock to grab. You know before you touch it roughly how heavy it will be and how it will flop. Your hand shapes itself on the way there. Your fingers squeeze exactly hard enough to hold it and not so hard that you tear it. If it slips, you have caught it before you consciously registered that it slipped. None of that feels like thinking, because you are not doing it consciously. But that machinery is the product of hundreds of millions of years of evolution, refined across an unimaginable span of time in every creature that had to see, grab, and move in order to stay alive. It is old, it is deep, and it runs so smoothly that it is invisible to the person using it. That is Moravec's point, and it is a point about us rather than about machines. We badly misjudge which of our own abilities are impressive. The recent skills, the ones we had to invent and can feel ourselves straining at, look like intelligence. The ancient ones, handed to us finished, look like nothing at all. So we built machines that beat us at the recent things first, and we are still working on the sock. There has been real progress. Robots now fold laundry, sort recycling, and pick fruit, and they manage it by learning from enormous piles of examples rather than by being handed the rules, because nobody can write the rules for a sock. But watch one work and you will see the paradox holding its ground. It is slow. It is careful. It fails in ways a four year old would not. The next time a machine does something clever and it unsettles you, it is worth remembering which way around the difficulty actually runs.
